title: Cache Basics — Hits & Misses
summary: The cache line, the hit/miss mechanics, and the single-level AMAT formula every later cache topic builds on.

slides.subTitle: Cache lines and blocks
slides.markdown:
A cache never moves single bytes between itself and memory — it moves fixed-size chunks called **cache lines** or **blocks**, typically 64 bytes on modern CPUs.

When the CPU asks for one byte and it's not in cache, the whole 64-byte-aligned line containing that byte gets fetched and stored. This is the mechanism that turns spatial locality into real performance: the next few bytes you touch are very likely already in that same line, so they hit for free.

slides.subTitle: Why the gap is so large
slides.markdown:
A **hit** means the requested data is already in cache — served in a handful of cycles. A **miss** means it isn't, so the CPU must fetch the containing line from a slower level (another cache level, or RAM), often 10–100x slower than a hit.

That asymmetry is why cache design obsesses over avoiding misses rather than merely speeding up hits: a hit is already fast, but a miss is where all the time goes. A handful of misses can dominate the runtime of a loop that mostly hits.

slides.subTitle: Hit rate and miss rate
slides.markdown:
**Hit rate** = hits ÷ total accesses; **miss rate** = 1 − hit rate. These are the numbers most cache discussions lead with, because they compress an entire access pattern into one comparable figure.

But a rate alone hides the *cost* of a miss. Two caches can both report 95% hit rate and perform very differently if one's misses are twice as expensive — which is exactly why AMAT (next) exists as the more complete metric.

slides.subTitle: Average Memory Access Time
slides.markdown:
**AMAT** (single level) = `Hit time + Miss rate × Miss penalty`.

`Hit time` is the cost paid on every access; `Miss rate × Miss penalty` is the extra cost paid only on the fraction of accesses that miss. AMAT folds both hit cost and miss cost into one number in the same units (cycles or nanoseconds), which is what actually predicts real performance — hit rate alone can't.

slides.subTitle: Hit and miss paths
slides.markdown:
A memory request takes one of two paths through the cache.

![A memory request flowing through cache, hitting or fetching a block on a miss](assets/hit-miss-flow.svg)

On a hit, the value returns immediately from the cache array. On a miss, the cache first fetches the containing block from the next level down, installs it, *then* returns the requested value — the extra round trip is the miss penalty.

assets.alt: A memory request flowing through cache, hitting or fetching a block on a miss

slides.subTitle: A worked example
slides.markdown:
```text
Address trace: A, B, A, C, A, B   (cache starts empty)
A -> miss (fetch)
B -> miss (fetch)
A -> hit
C -> miss (fetch)
A -> hit
B -> hit

Hits = 3, Misses = 3, Total = 6
Hit rate = 3 / 6 = 50%
```

Even this tiny trace shows the pattern: the first touch of any address is always a miss (nothing to reuse yet); only repeat touches can hit. Real programs get far higher hit rates because they repeat far more than 3 unique addresses.

slides.subTitle: Hit rate isn't the whole story
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A 99% hit rate is always better than a 90% hit rate."

**Why it's wrong:** hit rate says nothing about *miss penalty*. A 99% hit-rate design with a 400-cycle penalty can lose to a 90% hit-rate design with a 50-cycle penalty: `0.01×400=4` vs `0.10×50=5` extra cycles — close, and real penalty gaps are often bigger, easily flipping the comparison.

**Correct model:** always compare AMAT, not hit rate alone. A bigger, slower cache can raise hit rate while making AMAT worse.
